source.title: Low-Bit Quantization Favors Undertrained LLMs: Scaling Laws for Quantized LLMs with 100T Training Tokens
source.authors: Xu Ouyang; Tao Ge; Thomas Hartvigsen; Zhi-Song Zhang; Hai-Tao Mi; Dong Yu

page_placements.theme: Precision and compression penalties depend on size and training intensity

record.tranche_reason: The study fits a conventional cross-entropy scaling relationship on Pythia checkpoints, but its main experiments measure quantization-induced loss degradation rather than reproducing the original scaling-law studies.
record.gate_note: The fitted 16-bit loss relationship in Figure 7 bears on V1. The paper's main QiD fits are recorded as findings about a related but different measure, not as evidence for the original loss-law versions. Its 100-trillion-token results are projections, not observed runs; they do not test extrapolation against actual larger runs or a compute-optimal allocation.
record.test_reason: The paper's own results concern quantization-induced degradation (QiD), a different quantity from pretraining loss. It fits the Kaplan-form 16-bit loss law on Pythia only as a tool for predicting quantized loss. It reports no goodness-of-fit, residuals or exponent comparison for that 16-bit law; the 'fits well' statement refers to the Lossq predictions in Figure 7. The fit also uses intermediate checkpoints of fixed-schedule Pythia runs rather than separately trained runs. So the paper's results do not bear on whether V1 holds, and no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but incomplete. The authors conclude that low-bit quantization favours undertrained LLMs: QiD grows with training tokens and shrinks with model size and bit width. They propose QiD as a signal of how fully a model is trained. Their projections suggest low-bit quantization may be undesirable for models trained on about 100T tokens. They make no claims about conventional loss laws.
record.recipe_differences: The paper fits a conventional loss relationship on Pythia, but its main method and results concern GPTQ and other quantization methods and their loss degradation, rather than reproducing the original scaling-law experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: For the QiD fit, the reported fitted laws differ slightly across GPTQ, AWQ, and bitsandbytes; the paper also compares RefinedWeb with Wikitext-2 and reports nearly identical QiD results on those test datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: QiD is fitted by Δq Loss = 0.017·D^0.5251/(N^0.2261·P^5.4967) on GPTQ-quantized Pythia checkpoints. The separate per-factor fits give β=0.5316, α=0.2276 and γ=5.4812, close to the joint fit.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Post-training quantization degradation grows as a power of training tokens and shrinks as powers of model size and bit width.

fits_no_version.finding: The fitted 4-bit QiD laws differ across GPTQ, AWQ and bitsandbytes (e.g. D exponent 0.655, 0.595, 0.574; N exponent 0.384, 0.399, 0.284). The QiD trends themselves are described as almost identical.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: QiD scaling exponents depend on the quantization method.

fits_no_version.finding: The same QiD functional form is fitted on the Spectra suite and on Llama and Qwen models, where predicted QiD is compared with actual QiD (Figure 10). No numbers are given in the text.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The QiD scaling form transfers across model families.

fits_no_version.finding: Native 1.58-bit BitNet matches or beats bf16 training loss early in training, then lags behind; the gap appears later for the 1.2B model than for the 120M model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The gap between native low-bit and bf16 training loss grows with training tokens.

record.code_released: https://huggingface.co/Xu-Ouyang (quantized checkpoints; code release not stated)
record.problems: The conventional loss fit is reported for Pythia only, with sizes up to 12B and training up to approximately 206 billion tokens. The 100-trillion-token analysis is a projection, not an observed validation run. The evaluation uses 1,000 sampled texts, and the paper reports no uncertainty estimates for the fitted laws.
record.rows_left_out: No additional eligible rows omitted. Projections in Figure 1 and Table 1 are not observed outcomes; other QiD plots and comparisons either show the same aggregate trend or concern quantization degradation rather than the loss-law versions.

untested.parts: No test of the power-law fit to pretraining loss. The 16-bit fit is used as a tool, with no fit quality or comparison reported.
No comparison of small-run predictions with observed larger runs. The 100T-token results are QiD projections only.
No other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer. QiD and BitNet results are a different construct.
Fit differences are reported only for QiD laws across quantization methods, not for pretraining-loss laws.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' and V1 'supports' label are not justified. The conventional L(N,D) fit is an auxiliary tool with no reported validation. It also uses intermediate checkpoints of single training runs, a setup known to bias loss-law fits. Relation is downgraded to uses_without_test, T4, with no verdicts.

versions.untested_parts: The reported conventional loss fit jointly varies model size and training tokens; it does not report a compute scaling law or isolate all three axes under explicitly non-bottleneck conditions.
No comparison of predictions from small runs with observed runs orders of magnitude larger; the 100-trillion-token results are projections.
No fixed-compute sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation is reported.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The native low-bit training comparison does not fit or test power-law scaling; no other modalities, repeated-data scaling, fine-tuning, or transfer scaling is tested.
No downstream-task performance scaling or prediction is tested.
The study reports differing fits for quantization-induced degradation across quantization methods, not setup-dependent exponents or compute-optimal splits for the claimed pretraining-loss laws.
